edges.description: Loss of the oxaloacetate-to-phosphoenolpyruvate step directly interrupts flux through gluconeogenesis.
Because PEPCK-C is the route by which oxaloacetate exits the tricarboxylic acid cycle for glucose synthesis, its loss blocks this cataplerotic drain.
Once glycogen is depleted, the blocked gluconeogenic pathway cannot sustain blood glucose during fasting.

intermediate_mechanisms: Reduced endogenous glucose output lowers fasting tolerance, so adequate growth depends on frequent exogenous caloric intake.

edges.description: Severe or prolonged hypoglycemia deprives the brain of its principal fuel.

intermediate_mechanisms: Repeated encephalopathic crises cause neuroregression, leaving lasting global developmental delay.
Nitrogen that cannot be disposed of through gluconeogenic amino acid utilization is buffered as glutamine.
Hepatocellular dysfunction during acute decompensation impairs ureagenesis and nitrogen disposal, allowing ammonia to accumulate.

edges.description: Increased gluconeogenic demand during catabolic stress converts the compensated state into symptomatic hypoglycemia.
Hepatic PEPCK-C loss produces the hypoglycemia of gluconeogenic failure, and liver-specific reexpression rescues it.
edges.limitations: The whole-body knockout is neonatally lethal with profound hypoglycemia, unlike the viable, episodic, catabolism-triggered human disease, so the model reproduces the severe hepatic-gluconeogenesis phenotype but not the human clinical spectrum.

edges.description: Rising lactate reports accumulation of gluconeogenic carbon proximal to the PEPCK-C step.

nodes.description: Biallelic loss-of-function PCK1 variants deplete cytosolic phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK-C) activity. The enzyme catalyzes the GTP-dependent decarboxylation and phosphorylation of oxaloacetate to phosphoenolpyruvate, the first committed and rate-limiting cytosolic step of gluconeogenesis. Expression of a mutant allele in COS-1 cells produced an enzyme incapable of normal function, confirming the variants as loss-of-function.
